Although primary word stress is not predictable in Guayabero — the syllable bearing primary word stress can occur word initially, medially, or finally with no cooccurrence restrictions — it always occurs on either the ultimate or penultimate syllable of the grammatical stem, thereby identifying the stem in speech. Furthermore, syllable-final consonant clusters occur only in stem-final syllables bearing primary stress, so the maximum expansion of a syllable is always associated with primary stress. new_statements.translation: 3. Stress. The phonemic status of stress is established by the following contrasts: /pasá/ 'swamp' /pása/ 'to arrive' ... /nehéla/ 'new' /nehelá/ 'your hair' /ámo/ 'you should say' /amá/ 'here it is' ... /asá/ 'other' /ǽsa/ 'fish-hook'. [fn. 2:] In general terms affixation does not affect the stress. The authors suspended their research before they could define the basis for the change in stress placement when it occurs. ... [p. 54, 4.2:] The phonological word consists of one to five syllables. It is marked by potential pause, prenuclear increase in tempo, and a nucleus characterised by primary stress and simultaneous high pitch: /ben/ 'cassava bread' /mɨ́ntat/ 'in the water' /pihimélisdoʔ/ 'again'.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog record (Keels 1985: contrastive, not predictable): Waller & Waller establish stress as phonemic with minimal pairs on di- and trisyllables (pasa/pasa, nehela/nehela, amo/ama, asa/aesa) and write it in the orthography as an acute. They state no window and no default position; compatible detail added: the phonological word (1-5 syllables) has one nucleus with primary stress and simultaneous high pitch, affixation ('anexion') generally does not move the stress, and stress conditions segmental allophony (theta for /d/ after stressed vocoids, lax [open o] in unstressed syllables). One of their phonological-word examples, /pihimelisdo?/ 'de nuevo', carries the primary stre…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is phonemic (lexically contrastive): minimal pairs differ only in stress position, on disyllables and trisyllables, so its position is not predictable and it is written with an acute accent in the practical orthography. Each phonological word (1-5 syllables) has one primary-stressed nucleus, realised with simultaneous high pitch; affixation generally leaves the stress in place (unexplained exceptions noted). No fixed position, window or weight condition is stated.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated (only one primary-stress nucleus per phonological word is described; phrase-level pitch patterns are treated separately in 4.3).
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 2 (p. 52): affixation generally does not affect stress, but some stress shifts under affixation occur whose conditioning the authors could not determine before suspending fieldwork ('nuevos estudios.. seran publicadas en fecha proxima').
new_statements.identity_note: Guayabero (jiw), Guahiboan, spoken on the Guaviare river (Meta/Guaviare, Colombia); Tobar Ortiz 2000 maps the settlements Cano Ceiba, Barrancon, La Sal, Barranco Colorado, Mucuare, Laguna Barajas and notes an older vs younger speakers' pronunciation difference. Waller & Waller 1976 and Kondo 1998 are SIL-Colombia (Lomalinda) descriptions of the same language; no dialect split is at issue.

sources.quote: A pesar de que el acento primario de palabra no es predecible en guayabero --la sílaba que posee acento primario puede ocurrir al comienzo de la palabra, en el medio de ésta, o al final, y no hay restricciones co-ocurrentes-- siempre se presenta, o bien en la última sílaba, o en la penúltima de la raíz gramatical, identificando en esta forma la raíz. Además, agrupaciones de consonantes de final de sílaba ocurren únicamente en sílabas de final de raíz que llevan acento primario; así que la máxima expansión de la sílaba está siempre asociada con el acento primario. [...] Dentro de una palabra, cualquier sílaba contigua a la sílaba nuclear no lleva acento. Cualesquier otras sílabas pre-nucleares se presentan como dobletes --pares de sílabas compuestos de una sílaba con acento secundario y una sílaba sin acento, que alternan en secuencia-- precediendo a la sílaba nuclear. Siguiendo a ésta, no obstante, cualesquier sílabas adicionales serán también no acentuadas, exceptuando la sílaba final de la palabra, que lleva acento secundario. [...] La sílaba que lleva el acento primario es marcada por intensidad, un tono más alto, duración prolongada y el concomitante cambio en calidad de vocal

tone.quote: [p. 600, 4.1 Fonología] Esta presentación de la fonología en guayabero dará un inventario de los fonemas consonánticos y vocálicos, sus variantes alofónicas, una introducción a la estructura de la sílaba, y mostrará el acento como elemento suprasegmental en dicha lengua. [p. 602] 4.1.3. Suprasegmento. Respecto al acento, por ahora se puede señalar que tiene estatus fonológico, en cuanto que no es predecible su aparición. Sin embargo, se puede señalar una zona acentual bien definida, como lo son la última y la penúltima sílaba. Según ya se había anotado (cfr 4.1.2.2.), el acento como rasgo prosódico produce efectos fonéticos determinantes en esta lengua.
tone.locator: p. 600 (sec. 4.1, left column below the settlement map) and p. 602 (sec. 4.1.3, bottom of left column) of the Caro y Cuervo portal reissue
tone.translation: [4.1] This presentation of Guayabero phonology will give an inventory of the consonant and vowel phonemes, their allophonic variants, an introduction to syllable structure, and will show accent as the suprasegmental element in this language. [4.1.3] Suprasegment. As for accent, for now it can be said that it has phonological status, in that its position is not predictable. However, a well-defined accent zone can be identified, namely the last and penultimate syllables.
